extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent practitioners, USPTO examiners, and policymakers interested in 35 U.S.C. § 101 subject-matter-eligibility guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and applying USPTO guidance and examiner procedures for determining patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, including the multi-stage tests (statutory categories, judicial exceptions, inventive concept/practical application) and administrative rulemaking practices surrounding such guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1996 Guidelines: endorsement of Freeman-Walter-Abele test for algorithmic processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1996 Examination Guidelines for Computer-Related Inventions explicitly endorse a particular test (the Freeman-Walter-Abele test) for analyzing claims directed 'solely' to a process for solving algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance endorses that test as the Office's position on certain patentability standards for computer-related inventions. The final guidance was responsive to public comments, but it also explicitly rejected broad categorical presumptions (e.g., data structures per se or computer programs per se as statutory subject matter). It also sets forth a series of steps for examiners to follow when examining computer-related inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of business-method claims (1996 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Business method claims should be treated 'like any other process claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office admonished examiners to analyze business-method claims using the same framework applied to other process claims rather than applying a distinct standard that singles out business methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2005 Interim Guidelines: determine statutory category first; burden on USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading the application and considering the breadth of § 101, examiners are instructed first to 'determine whether the claimed invention falls within an enumerated statutory category.' The guidance notes the 'burden is on the USPTO to set forth a prima facie case of unpatentability' and that an examiner must explain a rejection only if 'it is more likely than not that the claimed subject matter falls outside all of the statutory categories.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners need not obsess over precisely classifying ambiguous instances into one of the four statutory categories; the standard for the examiner to justify a rejection is a prima facie showing that the claim falls outside the statutory classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2005 Interim Guidelines: judicial exceptions and practical application tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must determine whether the claimed invention falls within judicial exceptions to § 101: 'abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and laws of nature.' To surmount a judicial exception by virtue of a practical application, an invention must either (i) 'transform[] an article or physical object to a different state or thing' or (ii) 'otherwise produce[] a useful, concrete and tangible result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance emphasizes practical application as a path to eligibility and cites Diehr/Gottschalk support. It also explicitly rejects certain earlier tests (including the one earlier endorsed in 1996) as improper. The practical-application routes were presented as ways that inventions employing judicial-exception subject matter may nevertheless be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2009/2010 Interim Guidance: factors (including machine-or-transformation) as non-dispositive investigative tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2009/2010 interim instructions present a series of examples and factors—'inquiries gleaned from Supreme Court precedent' including machine-or-transformation inquiries—that speak in favor of or against patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document stresses these factors are a 'useful investigative tool,' not mandatory or dispositive; the list is non-exhaustive and nothing on it is dispositive. The guidance does not mandate a particular test or change the basic procedure but offers a 'cheat sheet' of considerations examiners might weigh.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2014 Interim Guidance / 2-part Mayo/Alice-based analysis (Step 2A & 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2014 guidance sets forth a two-part analysis for judicial exceptions: Step 1 — determine whether the claim is in a statutory category; Step 2A — is the claim 'directed to' a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea; Step 2B — do additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (the 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance includes a flowchart, nonlimiting lists of examples for Step 2A (with judicial citations), emphasizes that 'it is important to consider the claim as a whole' and 'every claim must be examined individually,' and provides examples of language found sufficient or insufficient for Step 2B. It also permits streamlined analyses for claims that 'clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception' (self-evident eligibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2015 Update: abstract-idea examples and instructive positions on MDC and evidentiary practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The July 2015 update listed specific abstract-idea categories (e.g., fundamental economic practices; certain methods of organizing human activity; an idea of itself; mathematical relationships/formulas) and synthesized public comments into themes. It also took a position on where markedly different characteristics (MDC) analysis belongs in the framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The update rejected moving the MDC analysis from Step 2A to Step 2B (observing that such reordering could change eligibility outcomes for some claims). It also instructed that findings that elements are 'well-understood, routine, or conventional' need not be supported by evidentiary submissions—judicial notice based on knowledge of those in the art or prior court cases is adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: May 2016 memorandum: process for rejecting claims under updated guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A May 2016 update (memorandum to the Patent Examining Corps) focused on the procedural aspects of issuing rejections under the subject-matter-eligibility guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memorandum addressed how examiners should document and carry out rejections under the then-current guidance (procedural emphasis rather than substantive change).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2018 Berkheimer Memorandum: factual findings and evidence requirement for Step 2B rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Berkheimer (which held that whether a claim element is 'well understood, routine, or conventional' is a question of fact), the USPTO instructed that examiners could not reject a claim under Step 2B without making a clear factual finding supported by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memorandum specified four categories of evidence (the memo required at least one of these categories be used to support any rejection). This raised the evidentiary bar for examiners and made it more difficult to sustain ineligibility rejections absent factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 Revised Guidance: grouping abstract ideas into three categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2019 guidance revised Step 2A by explaining that 'abstract ideas can be grouped' into three groupings: '[m]athematical concepts,' '[c]ertain methods for organizing human activity,' and '[m]ental processes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office stated these groupings 'extract and synthesize key concepts identified by the courts as abstract ideas.' The document does not cite a statute or single judicial source as the origin of the grouping—rather, it is an Office synthesis intended to make the increasing caselaw more tractable for examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 Revised Guidance: two-prong 'directed to' inquiry and practical-application carve-out
rubrics_metrics.description: The revised Step 2A implements a two-pronged inquiry: (prong 1) does the claim recite a judicial exception (using the new groupings), and (prong 2) is the claim 'directed to' that judicial exception. A claim that integrates the judicial exception into a practical application is not 'directed to' the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach creates a carve-out whereby claims that recite judicial-exception subject matter nonetheless are eligible if they integrate that matter into a practical application; it effectively shifts some 'practical application' considerations from Step 2B into Step 2A (a substantive change from earlier MPEP wording).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and role of examples and examiner training materials
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidance documents are frequently accompanied by voluminous examples, training materials, slide decks, worksheets with answer keys, transcripts, and compendia of examples and cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples and training units play an important role in shaping examiner practice and understanding; some documents merely summarize cases without distilling guidance, while others provide practical exam-plenary materials. Examples have been used to illustrate application of the framework to Supreme Court and Federal Circuit fact patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance publication practice and responsiveness to comments as indicators of substantive rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office posts guidance in a mix of venues (Federal Register, Official Gazette, USPTO website), sometimes requests comments, and variably responds to comments — practices that inform judgments about whether guidance functions like substantive rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency of publication venue and meaningful engagement with public comments are seen as indicia of stronger rulemaking practice; uneven responsiveness (interim documents left unaddressed vs. others revised with detailed responses) affects assessments of the Office's competence and of whether it is effectively engaging in substantive rulemaking without the procedural trappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial deference to USPTO guidance (Chevron vs Skidmore distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only rules receive Chevron deference; the Federal Circuit has held that because the USPTO lacked substantive rulemaking power in this area, 'the rule of controlling deference set forth in Chevron does not apply.' Guidance may be entitled to persuasive (Skidmore) weight, not Chevron deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may treat USPTO guidance as persuasive authority, but the Federal Circuit has been reluctant to even afford Skidmore deference in some contexts (e.g., Cleveland Clinic), emphasizing the need for consistent application of case law. The degree of deference afforded to guidance affects its practical bindingness and the policy tradeoffs for the agency.
